Jacob indeed, inasmuch as he was docile and ready to yield obedience to God, did not need to be impelled by force and terror; yet, because he was a man encompassed with flesh, it was profitable for him that he should be affected as with the glory of a present God, in order that the word might penetrate more effectually into his heart. It is, however, proper to recall to memory what I have said before, that the word was joined with it; because a silent vision would have profited little or nothing. We know that superstition eagerly snatches at mere spectres; by which means it presents God in a form of its own. But since no living image of God can exist without the word, whenever God has <hi type="italic">appeared</hi> to his servants, he has also <hi type="italic">spoken</hi> to them. Wherefore, in all outward signs, let us be ever attentive to his voice, if we would not be deluded by the wiles of Satan. But if those visions, in which the majesty of God shines, require to be animated by the word, then they who obtrude signs, invented at the will of men, upon the Church, exhibit nothing else than the empty pomps of a profane theater. Just as in the Papacy, those things which are called sacraments, are lifeless phantoms which draw away deluded souls from the true God. Let this mutual connection, then, be observed, that the vision which gives greater dignity to the word, precedes it; and that the word follows immediately, as if it were the soul of the vision. And there is no question that this was an appearance of the visible glory of God, which did not leave Jacob in suspense and hesitation; but which, by removing his doubt, firmly sustained him, so that he confidently embraced the oracle.<div eID="gen5669" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5668" osisID="Gen.46.2" type="section"/>
entries.f32a4fad4c21f29e69c9449050e9cd94924bffcf: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.3" sID="gen5670" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Jacob, Jacob</hi>. The design of the repetition was to render him more attentive. For, by thus familiarly addressing him, God more gently insinuates himself into his mind: as, in the Scripture, he kindly allures us, that he may prepare us to become his disciples. The docility of the holy man appears hence, that as soon as he is persuaded that God speaks, he replies that he is ready to receive with reverence whatever may be spoken, to follow wheresoever he may be called, and to undertake whatever may be commanded. Afterwards, a promise is added, by which God confirms and revives the faith of his servant. Whereas, the descent into Egypt was to him a sad event, he is bidden to be of good and cheerful mind; inasmuch as the Lord would always be his keeper, and after having increased him there to a great nation, would bring him back again to the place, whence he now compelled him to depart. And, indeed, Jacob’s chief consolation turned on this point; that he should not perpetually wander up and down as an exile, but should, at length, enjoy the expected inheritance. For, since the possession of the land of Canaan was the token of the Divine favor, of spiritual blessings, and of eternal felicity; if holy Jacob was defrauded of this, it would have availed him little or nothing to have riches, and all kinds of wealth and power heaped upon him, in Egypt. The return promised him is not, however, to be understood of his own person, but refers to his posterity. Now, as Jacob, relying on the promise, is commanded boldly to go down into Egypt; so it is the duty of all the pious, after his example, to derive such strength from the grace of God, that they may gird themselves to obey his commands. The title by which God here distinguishes himself, is attached to the former oracles which Jacob had received by tradition from his fathers. For why does he not rather call himself the Creator of heaven and earth, than the God of Isaac or of Abraham, except for this reason, that the dominion over the land of Canaan depends on the previous covenant, which he now ratifies anew? At the same time also, he encourages his servant by examples drawn from his own family, lest he should cease to proceed with constancy in his calling. For, when he had seen that his father Isaac, and had heard that his grandfather Abraham, though long surrounded by great troubles, never gave way to any temptations, it ill became him to be overcome by weariness in the same course; especially since, in the act of dying, they handed their lamp to their posterity, and took diligent care to leave the light of their faith to survive them in their family. In short, Jacob is taught that he must not seek, in crooked and diverse paths, that God whom he had learned, from his childhood, to regard as the Ruler of the family of Abraham; provided it did not degenerate from his piety. Moreover, we have elsewhere stated how far, in this respect, the authority of the Fathers ought to prevail. For it was not the design of God, either that Jacob should subject himself to men, or should approve, without discrimination, whatever was handed down from his ancestors, — seeing that he so often condemns in the Jews, a foolish imitation of their fathers, — but his design was to keep Jacob in the true knowledge of himself.<div eID="gen5671" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5670" osisID="Gen.46.3" type="section"/>
entries.cf1aca482644db3e26374a813152685dffa7fb1d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.4" sID="gen5672" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes</hi>. This clause was added for the sake of showing greater indulgence. For though Jacob, in desiring that, when he died, his eyes should be closed by the hand of Joseph, showed that some infirmity of the flesh was involved in the wish; yet God is willing to comply with it, for the sake of moderating the grief of a fresh banishment. Moreover, we know that the custom of closing the eyes was of the greatest antiquity; and that this office was discharged by one most closely connected with the deceased either by blood or affection.<div eID="gen5673" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5672" osisID="Gen.46.4" type="section"/>
entries.65cc172e32babf9b52ca2172bfda206bd3727e41: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.5" sID="gen5674" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Jacob rose up</hi>. By using the words “rose up,” Moses seems to denote that Jacob received new vigor from the vision. For although the former promises were not forgotten, yet the addition of the recent memorial came most opportunely, in order that he, bearing the land of Canaan in his heart, might endure his absence from it with equanimity. When it is said that he took with him all that he had acquired, or possessed in the land of Canaan, it is probable that his servants and handmaids came together with his cattle. <note n="178"> <div sID="gen5676" type="x-p"/> “A remarkable parallel to the description of the arrival of Jacob’s family in Egypt, is furnished by a scene in a tomb at Beni Hassan, representing strangers who arrive in Egypt. They carry their goods with them upon asses. The first figure is an Egyptian scribe, who presents an account of their arrival to a person in a sitting posture, one of the principal officers of the reigning Pharaoh — (compare the phrase, princes of Pharaoh, ver. 15.) The next, likewise an Egyptian, ushers them into his presence, and two of the strangers advance, bringing presents, the wild goat and the gazelle, probably as production of their country. Four men with bows and clubs follow, leading an ass, on which are two children in panniers, accompanied by a boy and four women. Last, another ass laden and two men, one of whom carries a bow and club, and the other a lyre, on which he plays with the plectrum. All the men have beards, contrary to the custom of the Egyptians,” etc. — Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 40. It is supposed by some that this sculpture was intended to represent the arrival of Jacob and his family, recorded in this chapter. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5676" type="x-p"/> </note> But, on his departure, no mention is made of them: nay, a little afterwards, when Moses enumerates the separate heads of each tribe, he says that only seventy souls came with him. Should any one say that Jacob had been compelled to liberate his slaves, on account of the famine, or that he lost them through some misfortune to us unknown, the conjecture is unsatisfactory; for it is most incredible that he, who had been an industrious master of a family, and had abounded in the earthly blessings of God, should have become so entirely destitute, that not even one little servant remained to him. It is more probable that, when the children of Israel were themselves employed in servile works, they were then deprived of their servants in Egypt; or, at least, a sufficient number was not left them, to inspire them with confidence in any enterprise. And although, in the account of their deliverance, Moses is silent respecting their servants, yet it may be easily gathered from other passages, that they did not depart without servants.<div eID="gen5675" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5674" osisID="Gen.46.5" type="section"/>
entries.5411e01df94e28f6c485cafb9622c8a780284426: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.8" sID="gen5677" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">These are the names of the children of Israel</hi>. He recounts the sons and grandsons of Jacob, till he arrives at their full number. The statement that there were but seventy souls, while Stephen (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.14">Acts 7:14</reference>) adds five more, is made, I doubt not, by an error of the transcribers. For the solution of Augustine is weak, that Stephen, by a prolepsis, enumerates also three who afterwards were born in Egypt; for he must then have formed a far longer catalogue. Again, this interpretation is repugnant to the design of the Holy Spirit, as we shall hereafter see: because the subject here treated of, is not respecting the number of children Jacob left behind him at his death, but respecting the number of his family on the day when he went down into Egypt. He is said to have brought with him, or to have found there, seventy souls born unto him, in order that the comparison of this very small number, with that immense multitude which the Lord afterwards led forth, might the more fully illustrate His wonderful benediction. But that the error is to be imputed to the transcribers, is hence apparent, that with the Greek interpreters, it has crept only into one passage, while, elsewhere, they agree with the Hebrew reckoning. And it was easy when numerals were signified by marks, for one passage to be corrupted. I suspect also that this happened from the following cause, that those who had to deal with the Scripture were generally ignorant of the Hebrew language; so that, conceiving the passage in the Acts to be vitiated, they rashly changed the true number. If any one, however, chooses rather to suppose that Luke in this instance accommodated himself to the rude and illiterate, who were accustomed to the Greek version, I do not contend with them. <note n="179"> <div sID="gen5679" type="x-p"/> Various methods have been resorted to, for the purpose of accounting for the difference of numbers given in this chapter and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.14">Acts 7:14</reference>. It is true that Luke, after the Septuagint, says there were seventy-five souls, whereas the Hebrew mentions only seventy. The reading of the Septuagint is, “The sons of Joseph, who were with him in Egypt, were nine souls; all of the souls of the house of Jacob which came with Jacob into Egypt, where seventy-five souls.” Add then nine to the sixty-six, mentioned in verse 26, and the number is made up. There is, however, some difficulty to make out the nine. — See <hi type="italic">Patrick</hi>, <hi type="italic">Poole</hi>, <hi type="italic">Bush</hi>, etc. in loc. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5679" type="x-p"/> </note> In the words of Moses there is, indeed, no ambiguity, nor is there any reason why so small a matter, in which there is no absurdity, should give us any trouble; for it is not wonderful, that, in this mode of notation, one letter should have been put in the place of another. It is more to the purpose, to examine wherefore this small number of persons is recorded by Moses. For, the more improbable it appears, that seventy men, in no lengthened space of time, should have grown to such a multitude; so much the more clearly does the grace of God shine forth. And this is also the reason why he so frequently mentions this number. For it was, by no means, according to human apprehension, a likely method of propagating the Church, that Abraham should live childless even to old age; that, after the death of Isaac, Jacob alone should remain; that he, being increased with a moderate family, should be shut up in a corner of Egypt, and that there an incredible number of people should spring up from this dry fountain. <note n="180"> <div sID="gen5680" type="x-p"/> From the date of God’s promise of a holy seed to Abraham, unto the birth of Isaac was twenty-five years. Isaac lived sixty years before Jacob was born. Jacob had nearly reached the age of eighty at the time of his marriage. So that about two hundred and forty years elapsed before more than two persons were born of a family which was to be as the stars of heaven, and as the sand on the sea-shore, for multitude! — See <hi type="italic">Bush</hi> in loc. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5680" type="x-p"/> </note> When Moses declares that Shaul, one of the sons of Simon, was born of a Canaanitish woman, while he does not even mention the mothers of the other sons, his intention, I doubt not, is to fix a mark of dishonor on his race. For the holy Fathers were on their guard, not to mix in marriage with that nation, from which they were separated by the decree of heaven. When Moses, having put down the names of Leah’s sons, says there were thirty-three souls, whereas he has only mentioned thirty-two; I understand that Jacob himself is to be reckoned the first in order. The statement that he had so many sons or daughters by Leah does not oppose this conclusion. For although, strictly speaking, his discourse is concerning sons, yet he commences with the head of the family. I reject the interpretation of the Hebrews, who suppose Jochebed the mother of Moses to be included, as being overstrained. A question suggests itself concerning the daughters, whether there were more than two. If Dinah alone were named, it might be said that express mention was made of her, because of the notorious fact which had happened to her. But since Moses enumerates another female in the progeny of Aser, I rather conjecture that these had remained unmarried, or single; for no mention is made of those who were wives.<div eID="gen5678" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5677" osisID="Gen.46.8" type="section"/>
entries.e2402d3fc34c3360929f827c09d75717c2178d90: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.28" sID="gen5681" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">And he sent Judah before him unto Joseph</hi>. Because Goshen <note n="181"> <div sID="gen5683" type="x-p"/> Though Moses does not describe in express ferms the position of the land of Goshen; yet the incidental allusions contained in the narrative, are sufficient to fix its locality; and the fact that those allusions are such as could only be made by a writer conversant with its peculairities, affords decisive evidence of the veracity of Moses as a writer of history.<div eID="gen5683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5684" type="x-p"/>The land of Goshen appears as the eastern border-land of Egypt; for on this side Jacob’s family entered, see <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.28">ver. 28</reference>.<div eID="gen5684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5685" type="x-p"/>It appears as lying near the chief city of Egypt, (see <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.10">Genesis 45:10</reference>.) What that city was, may be inferred from <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.13.22">Numbers 13:22</reference>, which points to Zoan or Tanis. This implies, that Zoan was one of the oldest cities of Egypt, and that it held the first rank. God is said to have performed his “wonders in the field of Zoan,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.12 Bible:Ps.78.43">Psalm 78:12, 43</reference>,) alluding to the plagues of Egypt.<div eID="gen5685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5686" type="x-p"/>The land of Goshen is described as pasture land, and, As one of the most fruitful regions of Egypt.<div eID="gen5686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5687" type="x-p"/>“All these circumstances harmonize, and the different points, discrepant as they may seem, find their application, when we fix upon the land of Goshen as the region east of the Tanitic arm of the Nile, as far as the isthmus of Suez, or the border of the Arabian desert.” — See Egypt and the Books of Moses, pp. 43-45. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5687" type="x-p"/> </note> had been selected by Joseph as the abode of his father and his brethren, Jacob now desires, that, on his coming, he may find the place prepared for him: for the expression which Moses uses, implies, not that he requires a house to be built and furnished for him, but only that he may be permitted there to pitch his tent without molestation. For it was necessary that some unoccupied place should be assigned him; lest, by taking possession of the pastures or fields of the inhabitants, he might give them an occasion for exciting a tumult.<div eID="gen5682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5688" type="x-p"/>In the meeting of Jacob with his son Joseph, Moses describes their vehement feeling of joy, to show that the holy Fathers were not destitute of natural affection. It must, however, be remembered that, although the affections spring from good principles, yet they always contract some evil, from the corrupt propensity of the flesh; and have chiefly this fault, that they always exceed their bounds: whence it follows, that they do not need to be eradicated, but to be kept within due bounds.<div eID="gen5688" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5681" osisID="Gen.46.28" type="section"/>
entries.494aeb67686bf3434cef6f89f8276a7384c42b16: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.46.31" sID="gen5689" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31. </hi><hi type="italic">I will go up and show Pharaoh</hi>. After Joseph had gone forth to meet his father for the purpose of doing him honor, he also provides what will be useful for him. On this account, he advises Jacob to declare that he and all his family were keepers of cattle, to the end that he might obtain, from the king, a dwelling-place for them, in the land of Goshen. Now although his moderation deserves commendation on the ground, that he usurps no authority to himself, but that, as one of the common people, he waits the pleasure of the king: he yet may be thought craftily to have devised a pretext, by which he might circumvent the king. We see what he desired. Seeing that the land of Goshen was fertile, and celebrated for its rich pastures; this advantage so allured his mind, that he wished to fix his father there: but then, keeping out of Pharaoh’s sight the richness of the land, he puts forth another reason; namely, that Jacob with his sons, were men held in abomination, and that, therefore, he was seeking a place of seclusion, in which they might dwell apart from the Egyptians. It is not, however, very difficult to untie this knot. The fertility of the land of Goshen was so fully known to the king, that no room was left for fraud or calming, (though kings are often too profuse, and foolishly waste much, because they know not what they grant,) yea, Pharaoh, of his own accord, had offered them, unsolicited, the best and choicest place in the kingdom. Therefore this bounty of his was not elicited from him by stratagem; because he was free to form his own judgment respecting what he would give. And truly Joseph, in order that he might act modestly, felt it necessary to seek a habitation in Goshen, on this pretext. For it would have been absurd, or at least inconsiderate, for men who were obscure and strangers, to desire an abode in the best and most convenient place for themselves, as if they possessed a right to choose for themselves. Joseph, therefore, having regard to his own modesty and that of his father, adduces another cause, which was yet a true one. For seeing that the Egyptians held the occupation of shepherds in abhorrence, <note n="182"> <div sID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> “The monuments even now furnish abundant evidence of this hatred of the Egyptians to shepherds. The artists of Upper and Lower Egypt vie with each other in caricaturing them. In proportion as the cultivation of the land was the more unconditionally the foundation of the Egyptian state, the idea of coarseness and barbarism was united with the idea of a shepherd among the Egyptians.” — Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 42. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> </note> he explains to the king that this would be a suitable retreat for his brethren. Herein was no dissimulation, because, in no other place, was a quiet habitation accessible to them. Nevertheless, though it was hard for the holy Fathers to be thus opprobriously rejected, and, as it were, to be loathed by a whole nation; yet this ignominy with which they were branded, was most profitable to themselves. For, had they been mingled with the Egyptians, they might have been scattered far and wide; but now, seeing that they are objects of detestation, and are thought unworthy to be admitted to common society, they learn, in this state of separation from others, to cherish more fervently mutual union between themselves; and thus the body of the Church, which God had set apart from the whole world, is not dispersed. So the Lord often permits us to be despised or rejected by the world, that being liberated and cleansed from its pollution, we may cultivate holiness. Finally, he does not suffer us to be bound by chains to the earth, in order that we may be borne upward to heaven.<div eID="gen5690" type="x-p"/><div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.46.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5689" osisID="Gen.46.31" type="section"/><div eID="gen5595"/><div eID="gen5593"/> <div sID="gen5692"/> <div sID="gen5693" type="x-p"/>CHAPTER 47.<div eID="gen5693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5694"/> <table> <row> <cell> <div sID="gen5695" type="x-p"/><reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.1-Gen.47.31">Genesis 47:1-31</reference><div eID="gen5695" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1 </hi>Then Joseph came and told Pharaoh, and said, My father and my brethren, and their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have, are come out of the land of Canaan; and, behold, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the land of Goshen.<div eID="gen5696" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi>Et venit Joseph, et nuntiavit Pharaoni, et dixit, Pater meus, et fratres mei, et pecudes eorum, et boves eorum, et omnia quae erant eis, venerunt e terra Chenaan: et ecce, sunt in terra Gosen.<div eID="gen5697" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2 </hi>And he took some of his brethren, <hi type="italic">even</hi> five men, and presented them unto Pharaoh.<div eID="gen5698" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2. </hi>Et de extremis fratribus suis cepit quinque viros, et statuit eos ante Pharaonem.<div eID="gen5699" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3 </hi>And Pharaoh said unto his brethren, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> your occupation? And they said unto Pharaoh, Thy servants <hi type="italic">are</hi> shepherds, both we, <hi type="italic">and</hi> also our fathers.<div eID="gen5700" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3. </hi>Tune dixit Pharao ad fratres ejus, Quae sunt opera vestra? Et dixerunt ad Pharaonem, Pastores ovium sunt servi tui, etiam nos, etiam patres, nostri.<div eID="gen5701" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4 </hi>They said moreover unto Pharaoh, For to sojourn in the land are we come; for thy servants have no pasture for their flocks; for the famine <hi type="italic">is</hi> sore in the land of Canaan: now therefore, we pray thee, let thy servants dwell in the land of Goshen.<div eID="gen5702" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4. </hi>Et dixerunt ad Pharaonem, Ut peregrinaremur in hac terra, venimus, quia non est pascuum pecudibus, quae sunt servis tuis: gravis enim fames est in terra Chenaan: nunc igitur habitent quaeso servi tui in terra Gosen.<div eID="gen5703" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5 </hi>And Pharaoh spake unto Joseph, saying, Thy father and thy brethren are come unto thee:<div eID="gen5704" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5. </hi>Et dixit Pharao ad Joseph, dicendo, Pater tuus et fratres tui venerunt ad to.<div eID="gen5705" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6 </hi>The land of Egypt <hi type="italic">is</hi> before thee; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell: and if thou knowest <hi type="italic">any</hi> men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.<div eID="gen5706" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6. </hi>Terra Aegypti coram to est, in optimo terrae hujus habitare fac patrem tuum, et fratres tuos, habitent in terra Gosen. Et si cognoveris quod sint inter eos viri robusti, pones eos praefectos pecorum super ea quae sunt mihi.<div eID="gen5707" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7 </hi>And Joseph brought in Jacob his father, and set him before Pharaoh: and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.<div eID="gen5708" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7. </hi>Postea adduxit Joseph ipsum Jahacob patrem suum, et statuit eum coram Pharaone, et salutavit Jahacob ipsum Pharaonem.<div eID="gen5709" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8 </hi>And Pharaoh said unto Jacob, How old <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou?<div eID="gen5710" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8. </hi>Et dixit Pharao ad Jahacob, Quot sunt dies annorum vitae tuae?<div eID="gen5711" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9 </hi>And Jacob said unto Pharaoh, The days of the years of my pilgrimage <hi type="italic">are</hi> an hundred and thirty years: few and evil have the days of the years of my life been, and have not attained unto the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage.<div eID="gen5712" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9. </hi>Et dixit Jahacob ad Pharaonem, Dies annorum peregrinationum mearum sunt triginta et centum anni: pauci et mali fuerunt dies annorum vitae meae, et non attigerunt dies annorum vitae patrum meorum in diebus peregrinationum suarum.<div eID="gen5713" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10 </hi>And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from before Pharaoh.<div eID="gen5714" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10. </hi>Et salutavit Jahacob ipsum Pharaonem, et egressus est a facie Pharaonis.<div eID="gen5715" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11 </hi>And Joseph placed his father and his brethren, and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.<div eID="gen5716" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11. </hi>Et habitare fecit Joseph patrem suum et fratres suos, et dedit eis possessionem in terra Aegypti, in optimo terrae, in terra Rahameses, quemadmodum praeceperat Pharao.<div eID="gen5717" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12 </hi>And Joseph nourished his father, and his brethren, and all his father’s household, with bread, according to <hi type="italic">their</hi> families.<div eID="gen5718" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12. </hi>Et aluit Joseph patrem suum, et fratres suos, et omnem domum patris sui pane, usque ad os parvuli.<div type="italic">was</hi> very sore, so that the land of Egypt and <hi type="italic">all</hi> the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine.<div eID="gen5720" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13. </hi>At panis non erat in omni terra: gravis enim fames erat valde, et elanguit terra Aegypti et terra Chenaan propter famem.<div eID="gen5721" omnem peeuniam, quae inventa est in terra Chenaan pro alimento quod ipsi emebant; et intulit Joseph pecuniam in domum Pharaonis.<div eID="gen5723" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15 </hi>And when money failed in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came unto Joseph, and said, Give us bread: for why should we die in thy presence? for the money faileth.<div eID="gen5724" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15. </hi>Et consumpta est pecunia e terra Aegypti, et e terra Chenaan: et venit omnis Aegyptus ad Joseph, dicendo, Da nobis panem: et utquid moriemur coram to? Defecit enim pecunia.<div eID="gen5725" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16 </hi>And Joseph said, Give your cattle; and I will give you for your cattle, if money fail.<div eID="gen5726" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> Tune dixit Joseph, Date pecudes vestras, et dabo vobis pro pecudibus vestris, si defecit pecunia.<div eID="gen5727" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17 </hi>And they brought their cattle unto Joseph: and Joseph gave them bread <hi type="italic">in exchange</hi> for horses, and for the flocks, and for the cattle of the herds, and for the asses: and he fed them with bread for all their cattle for that year.<div eID="gen5728" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17. </hi>Et adduxerunt pecudes suas ad Joseph, et dedit eis Joseph panem pro equis, et pro grege pecudum, et pro armento boum, et pro asinis: et sustentavit eos pane pro omnibus gregibus illorum anno ipso.<div eID="gen5729" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18 </hi>When that year was ended, they came unto him the second year, and said unto him, We will not hide <hi type="italic">it</hi> from my lord, how that our money is spent; my lord also hath our herds of cattle; there is not ought left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands:<div eID="gen5730" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18. </hi>Finitus vero est annus ipse, et venerunt ad eum anno secundo, et dixerunt ei, Non abscondemus a domino meo, quod integra pecunia, et grex jumentorum apud dominum meum: non remansit coram domino meo praeterquam corpus nostrum, et terra nostra.<div eID="gen5731" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19 </hi>Wherefore shall we die before thine eyes, both we and our land? buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants unto Pharaoh: and give <hi type="italic">us</hi> seed, that we may live, and not die, that the land be not desolate.<div eID="gen5732" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19. </hi>Utquid moriemur in oculis tuis, etiam nos, etiam terra nostra? Eme nos, et terram nostram pro pane, et vivemus nos et terra nostra servi Pharanois: da semen, et vivemus, et non moriemur, et terra non desolabitur.<div eID="gen5733" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20 </hi>And Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh; for the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them: so the land became Pharaoh’s.<div eID="gen5734" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20. </hi>Et emit Joseph omnem terram Aegypti pro Pharaone: vendiderunt enim Aegyptii unusquisque agrum suum, quia invaluerat super eos fames: et fuit terra ipsi Pharaoni.<div eID="gen5735" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21 </hi>And as for the people, he removed them to cities from <hi type="italic">one</hi> end of the borders of Egypt even to the <hi type="italic">other</hi> end thereof.<div eID="gen5736" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21. </hi>Et populum transire fecit ad urbes ab extremitate termini Aegypti usque ad extremitatem ejus.<div eID="gen5737" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22 </hi>Only the land of the priests bought he not; for the priests had a portion <hi type="italic">assigned them</hi> of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands.<div eID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22. </hi>Tantummodo terram sacerdotum non emit, quia pars sacerdotibus erat a Pharaone, et comedebant partem suam, quam dederat eis Pharao: idcirco non vendiderunt terram suam.<div eID="gen5739" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23 </hi>Then Joseph said unto the people, Behold, I have bought you this day and your land for Pharaoh: lo, <hi type="italic">here is</hi> seed for you, and ye shall sow the land.<div eID="gen5740" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23. </hi>Tunc dixit Joseph ad populum, Ecce, emi vos hodie, et terram vestram Pharaoni: ecce, vobis semen, et seretis terram.<div eID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24 </hi>And it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.<div eID="gen5742" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24. </hi>Et erit, e frugibus dabitis quintam partem Pharaoni, et quatuor partes erunt vobis pro semine agri, et pro cibo vestro, et eorum qui sunt in domibus vestris, et ad comedendum pro parvulis vestris.<div eID="gen5743" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25 </hi>And they said, Thou hast saved our lives: let us find grace in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.<div eID="gen5744" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25. </hi>Et dixerunt, Vivificasti nos: inveniamus gratiam in oculis domini mei, et erimus servi Pharaonis.<div eID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26 </hi>And Joseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Pharaoh should have the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi>; except the land of the priests only, <hi type="italic">which</hi> became not Pharaoh’s.<div eID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26. </hi>Et posuit illud Joseph in statutum usque ad diem hanc super terram Aegypti Pharaoni pro quinta parte, terra tamen sacerdotum duntaxat non fuit Pharaoni.<div eID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27 </hi>And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.<div eID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27. </hi>Et habitavit Israel in terra Aegypti, in terra Gosen: et stationem habuerunt in ea, et creverunt, et multiplicati sunt valde.<div eID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28 </hi>And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years: so the whole age of Jacob was an hundred forty and seven years.<div eID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi>Et vixit Jahacob in terra AEGypti septendecim annos: et fuerunt dies Jahacob anni vitae ejus, septem anni et quadraginta et centum anni.<div eID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29 </hi>And the time drew nigh that Israel must die: and he called his son Joseph, and said unto him, If now I have found grace in thy sight, put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh, and deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt:<div eID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29. </hi>Appropinquaverunt autem dies Israel ut moreretur, et vocavit filium suum Joseph, et dixit ei, Si quaeso inveni gratiam in oculis tuis, pone quaeso manum tuam sub femore meo, et facies medum misericordiam et veritatem, Ne quaeso sepelias me in Aegypto.<div eID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30 </hi>But I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their buryingplace. And he said, I will do as thou hast said.<div eID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30. </hi>Et dormiam cum patribus meis; et tolles me ex Aegypto, et sepelies me in sepulcro eorum. Et dixit, Ego faciam secundum verbum tuum.<div eID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31 </hi>And he said, Swear unto me. And he sware unto him. And Israel bowed himself upon the bed’s head.<div eID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> Et dixit, Jura mihi et juravit ei, et incurvavit se Israel ad caput lecti.<div eID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row> </table> <div sID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5758" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="46" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XLVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND Israel took his journey with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed sacrifices <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Both in thankfulness to God for former favours, and espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially for <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> preservation and happiness; and by way of supplication to God for his direction in this great case, whether he might leave the promised land of <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> and go into the idolatrous and impious land of <ns0:hi>Egypt;</ns0:hi> and for his protection and blessing as well in his journey as in <ns0:hi>Egypt.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> unto the God of his fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Isaac <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Whom <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> honoured and served, and who had constantly protected and provided for <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> and confirmed his covenant with him. He mentions <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> rather than <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> partly for <ns0:hi>Isaacs</ns0:hi> honour, to shew that though <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> was much inferiour to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> in gifts and graces, yet God was no less <ns0:hi>Isaacs</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> God, and therefore would be his God also notwithstanding his un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />worthiness: and partly for his own comfort, because <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>Iacobs</ns0:hi> immediate Parent and had transferred the blessing of the Covenant from <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and the validity of that transla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion depended upon <ns0:hi>Isaacs</ns0:hi> interest in God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) In that way or manner of visions which God afford<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to men by night and in their sleep. See <ns0:hi>Gen</ns0:hi> 20. 3. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 33. 15, 16. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 1. 20. and 2. 13, 19. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 16 9. and 18. 9, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and said, Jacob, Jacob <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He doubles the name both in token of his friend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship and familiarity with him and to raise <ns0:hi>Iacobs</ns0:hi> attention. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22, 11. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 10.</ns0:note>: And he said, here am I.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And he said, I am God, the God of thy fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, fear not <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For here were many causes of fear; lest he should do evil in forsaking the promised and blessed land, and going to a place which had been incommodious to his grandfather, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12. 15. and forbidden to his father. <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 2. lest he should expose his children to manifold perils, as, of being infected with the vices and particularly the Idolatry which reigned there above all other countries, and of being inveagled by the plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />santness and eminent fruitfulness of that soil to give up them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves to all manner of pleasures and to settle themselves there and give over all thoughts of returning to <ns0:hi>Canaan;</ns0:hi> and of be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing brought into that grievous bondage and affliction which was spoken of <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. 13. and lest some mischief should befal him or his in so long and dangerous a journey.</ns0:note> to go down into Egypt: for I will there make of thee a great nation.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 I will go down with thee into Egypt, and I will also surely bring thee up <ns0:hi>again</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Though not in thy person, yet in thy body, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 29, 30. and 50. 5, 13. and in thy posterity, which are a part of thy self, or thy self multiplyed.</ns0:note>: and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Shall close thy eyes; which office was usually performed by the nearest and dearest relations of the dying party among the <ns0:hi>Iews, Greeks</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi> Here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> is assured that he should die in peace, and that <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> both now was alive, and should survive his father.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 7. 15.</ns0:note> Jacob rose up from Beer-sheba: and the sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, and their little ones, and their wives in the wagons, which Pharaoh had sent to carry him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And they took their cattle, and their goods which they had gotten in the land of Canaan <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And in <ns0:hi>Mesopotamia.</ns0:hi> But <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> onely is here mentioned, because here they got the far greatest part of them, which by a Synecdoche is put for the whole.</ns0:note>, and came into Egypt, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 24. 4. Psal. 105. 23. Isa. 52. 4.</ns0:note> Jacob, and all his seed with him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 His sons, and his sons sons with him, his daughters <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either, his daughter, <ns0:hi>Dina<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> the plural number for the sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gular, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 23. <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21. 7. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 26. 8. or <ns0:hi>Dina<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> and her daughters; for grandchildren are commonly called their grand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fathers children or sons or daughters: or his daughters in law, his sons wives.</ns0:note>, and his sons daughters, and all his seed brought he with him into Egypt.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:43" />8 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 1. 1. and 6. 14. Numb. 26. 8. & 1 Chro. 5. 1.</ns0:note> these <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the names of the children of Israel which came into Egypt <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This Genealogy is both here and elsewhere described ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />actly and particularly, as well to shew the faithfulness of God in the performance of his promise concerning the vast multipli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation of <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> seed, and that in so short a time; as to di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stinguish the tribes; which was of great importance and ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary for the disposal of the Kingdome and Priesthood and a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove all for the discovery of the true <ns0:hi>Messias.</ns0:hi> Compare this following catalogue with that <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 26. and 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 6. and 7. and 8,</ns0:note>, Jacob and his sons: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Numb. 26. 5.</ns0:note> Reuben, Jacobs first born.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the sons of Reuben, Hanoch, and Phallu, and Hezron, and Carmi.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 6. 15. 1 Chron. 4. 24.</ns0:note> And the sons of Simeon: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Nemuel.</ns0:note> Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who is not mentioned in those parallel places, because he was then dead and that without issue.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Jarib.</ns0:note> Jachin, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Zerah.</ns0:note> Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which is here men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned as a brand upon him, and as an intimation that the rest of them, except <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> married to persons of a better race.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And the sons <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, 16.</ns0:note> of Levi, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Gershom.</ns0:note> Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And the sons of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 2. 3. and 4. 21. Chap. 38. 3.</ns0:note> Judah: Er, and Onan, and Shelah and Pharez, and Zerah, but Er, and Onan died in the land of Canaan <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">And therefore are contained in the following number, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15.</ns0:note>. And the sons of Pharez were <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 2. 5.</ns0:note> Hezron, and Hamul <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Who, though they seem to have been born in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> yet are here set down amongst those who came into <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gypt,</ns0:hi> because they came thither in their fathers loyns, as <ns0:hi>Levi</ns0:hi> is said <ns0:hi>to pay tithes in Abraham, Heb.</ns0:hi> 7. 9. And the children may as well be said to come thither in their Parents, as their father <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> is said to return from thence, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 4. in his children. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> If this be the sence, why should these two be mentioned rather than the grandchildren of the other brethren, who came into <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> in the same manner! <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> This may be done either, 1. From some special excellency or eminency in them above the rest, as <ns0:hi>Hezron</ns0:hi> was eminent for being the progenitour of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hamul</ns0:hi> might be so for some other cause though un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />known to us. Or 2. Because they were the first grand-children that were born in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and it may be all that were born whilst <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> lived there, and therefore are not unfitly named with <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> and allotted to him, as <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> two eldest sons <ns0:hi>Ephra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />im</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi> were by <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> appropriated to himself, and rec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />koned as his immediate sons, when all the rest of <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> sons were excluded from that priviledge, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 48. 5, 6. And the like may be said of the other two Grandchildren mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 7. 1.</ns0:note> the sons of Issachar: Tola and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or</ns0:hi> Puah, -Ja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shub.</ns0:note> Phu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vah, and Job, and Shimron.</ns0:p>
